references.text: Here the same Hebrew expression is used (וַיִּנָּחֶם יְהוָה) – the Lord regretted the evil he had planned to do to his people after Moses' intercession. This is the closest linguistic parallel to Genesis 6:6.
God says that he regrets (נחם) having made Saul king, because Saul has turned away. This is a direct parallel to God's regret over having created humans in Genesis 6:6.
The verse repeats that the Lord regretted having made Saul king over Israel and uses the same root (נחם) as in Genesis 6:6.
The psalmist describes how God remembered his covenant and relented (נחם) out of his great compassion, showing God's ability to change his course of action in response to people.

Jeremiah explains the principle that God can relent from the evil he has planned against a nation if they repent, and vice versa. This provides theological background for understanding God's regret in Genesis 6:6.
Isaiah describes how Israel's rebellion grieved (עצב) God's Holy Spirit, which connects to וַיִּתְעַצֵּב (he was grieved in his heart) in Genesis 6:6.
By faith Noah built an ark to save his family, an action that came as a result of God's judgment on humanity – a judgment motivated by God's sorrow and regret described in Genesis 6:6.
Creates a theological contrast between God's sorrow leading to judgment (Genesis) and God's compassion leading to salvation (Joel).
